column4: The exact و ر ي root of the source's مُورِيَات returns in the question about the fire تُورُونَ, the fire people make emerge.
The question whether people created the fire's tree or God locates the source behind the apparently human act of kindling.
God makes that fire both a reminder and a practical provision; this directly answers the section's distinction between a useful fire and the horse-spark that benefits no one.
Fire issuing from a green tree joins apparent opposites, and the surrounding resurrection argument turns ordinary kindling into evidence that life can issue from death.
Moses يَسْتَأْنِسُ a fire from the side of the mount and approaches for خَبَر or a firebrand, staging the source's ء ن س sense while linking the promised news to 100:11's خَبِير.
Moses says إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا and expects خَبَر or a شِهَابٍ قَبَسٍ; the seen flame joins the source's ء ن س sense, a portable ember, and the خ ب ر family of 100:11.
Moses's إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا leads him to seek a firebrand or guidance at the fire, realizing both the source's ء ن س sense and its question of what a spark will become.
On reaching the fire, Moses is called from a tree in the blessed place; the neighbour supplies both the news promised in 28:29 and a striking meeting of fire and tree.
Arrival at the fire yields a divine call, blessing, and glorification, showing that this distant flame gives far more than physical warmth or a passing spark.
When Moses reaches the fire he is called by name, the first concrete fulfilment of the guidance he hoped to find in 20:10.
A kindled fire briefly lights its surroundings before God takes the light and leaves darkness; it is the clearest Quranic boundary between momentary ignition and enduring illumination.
The source dictionary's مِصْبَاح appears in a niche, fueled by a blessed tree whose oil nearly shines without fire; sustained lamp-light answers the image's futile airborne sparks.
Metal is heated in fire, useless scum rises, and what benefits people remains; the verse gives the image's fleeting spark versus useful result a precise material analogue.
The deeds of rejecters become ashes driven violently by wind, making the source dictionary's dabh-as-ash into an image of an effort from which nothing can be retained.
وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ makes morning itself breathe, bringing the first ayah's breath and the third ayah's dawn together as darkness gives way.
Hoarded gold and silver are heated in Hell and used to brand bodies, joining love of wealth to the source's sense of fire scorching or branding what it touches.
The man فَكَّرَ وَقَدَّرَ, thinking and calculating before a disastrous judgment, directly enacts the source dictionary's figurative “striking” of a matter by examining and planning it.
Saqar is لَوَّاحَةٌ لِلْبَشَرِ, scorching or blackening human skin; this is the Quranic counterpart to the source's fire that changes a thing's colour.
The people of the Blaze admit that listening or reasoning would have kept them from it, directly joining misuse of the mind to a fire that is the outcome of that failure.
Iron blocks are blown upon until they become fire-hot, then covered with molten metal; iron, force, heat, and a useful finished work recast the section's physical ignition scene.
Hell throws out شَرَرٍ, sparks, giving a direct Quranic scene of fire scattering sparks through the air.
Hypocrites ask believers to wait so that they may نَقْتَبِسْ from their light, but no share is available; the sought qabas reverses Moses's successful quest for a firebrand and guidance.
“Be stones or iron” names the two materials of the section's fire-making tool inside a challenge about resurrection, joining its physical apparatus to the same proof made with fire in 36:80.
Moses burns the calf and then scatters it into the sea, a complete Quranic movement from burning an object to dispersing what remains.
نَارُ اللَّهِ الْمُوقَدَةُ is a deliberately kindled fire, and its placement after wealth-counting makes fire the end of a human project that was mistaken for lasting gain.
وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا repeats the surah's love-of-wealth sense of ح ب ب, the same family in which the source finds the useless horse-spark's name.
Wealth cannot benefit its owners against God and they become fuel for the Fire, tightly joining prized possessions, failed benefit, and fire.
Hell is heard شَهِيقًا as it boils, making breath and raging fire coincide just as the section hears heat and ash within the runners' breath.
God is فَالِقُ الْإِصْبَاحِ and appoints night for rest; the same ص ب ح family presents dawn as a divinely opened boundary after darkness.
The objection asks who can revive decayed bones, the precise resurrection denial to which the green-tree fire of 36:80 responds.
The answer points to the One who originated the bones the first time, stating the resurrection inference that the following fire-from-tree image makes perceptible.
The passage's skeptics ask whether death, dust, and bones can really be followed by resurrection; that is the objection addressed by the crop, water, and fire questions culminating in 56:71–73.
The first أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ question turns to what people till, opening the crop-water-fire sequence cited by the section.
The contrast between human sowing and God's causing growth establishes the same hidden agency later asked about the fire's tree.
The second أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ question turns to the water people drink, the middle member of the crop-water-fire proof named in the section.
As with the fire's tree, the verse asks whether people brought the water down or God did, exposing provision behind apparent human use.
God could make the water bitter; this counterfactual clarifies that usefulness is bestowed, preparing for the useful fire of 56:73.
The fire proof concludes with a command to glorify the name of the Supreme Lord, fixing the stance the preceding questions are meant to produce.
The human being forgets creation from a drop and becomes an open disputant, establishing why the bone question and fire answer are needed.
Creation of the heavens and earth is invoked as the larger measure of God's ability to recreate humans, continuing the inference begun with fire from green wood.
The resurrection proof closes by glorifying the One in whose hand is dominion and to whom all return, paralleling the doxological close of the fire sequence in 56:74.
Abu Lahab's wealth and gains do not benefit him, restating in personal form the section's pairing of coveted good with something ultimately useless.
He enters a fire of flame immediately after his wealth is declared useless, making the wealth–nonbenefit–fire sequence explicit.
Whenever opponents kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it; this is a direct reversal of the source dictionary's reviving of a dormant fire and of ignition that succeeds.
Whenever Hell subsides, God increases its blaze, a dark eschatological counterpart to the source dictionary's act of stirring a fading fire back into flame.
Moses sees a fire from far away and approaches it; here the Fire itself sees its people from a distant place and they hear its rage, reversing observer and observed as well as hoped-for benefit.
The guilty see the Fire and know they will fall into it with no escape, opposing Moses's hopeful sight of a distant fire that yields news and guidance.
A commanded strike on stone makes twelve springs burst out; the same hard contact with stone yields water rather than the fire produced in the section's striking scene.
The repeated Moses account again has a staff strike stone and water issue in twelve springs, a precise elemental reversal of striking stone for sparks.
In the warned-of Fire, people and stones are fuel; stone here sustains fire by being consumed rather than serving as the struck tool from which a spark escapes.
The Fire guarded by angels likewise has people and stones as fuel, turning the section's human use of stone for ignition into an eschatological reversal.
Lot is told that morning is his people's appointed time of destruction—“is morning not near?”—so the ص ب ح boundary brings judgment rather than simply secure daylight.
A settled punishment reaches Lot's people at morning; the same ص ب ح moment that displaces darkness in the section here makes the coming consequence endure.
After the call at the fire, God chooses Moses and commands him to listen to revelation, specifying the guidance that 20:10 only anticipated.
The guidance found at the fire becomes recognition of God, worship, and remembrance, giving the distant light a durable human consequence.
The caller at the fire identifies Himself as God, the Mighty and Wise, supplying the authoritative news for which Moses approached.
Remembering the first creation is offered as the inference the deniers should draw before the passage proceeds through seed, water, and fire.
God could reduce the crop to broken debris; within the sequence this supplies a non-fire analogue to the source's progression from heat to residue.
God's command “Be” explains how re-creation follows from the power illustrated by fire issuing from green wood.
ثُمَّ نَظَرَ continues the deliberate looking named in the source dictionary, while its place in the sequence shows that scrutiny alone does not ensure a sound result.
The man's deliberation produces the false verdict that revelation is transmitted magic, the failed intellectual “spark” anticipated by the section.
Calling revelation merely human speech completes the wrong conclusion reached after thought and inspection.
The response “I will burn him in Saqar” joins the preceding corrupt deliberation to the fire later described as scorching skin.
Collecting and repeatedly counting wealth supplies the human project whose imagined gain ends in the kindled fire of 104:6.
The wealth-counter thinks his property has made him last forever, directly opposing the section's question of what momentary effort can truly endure.
The kindled fire rises over hearts, turning the fire image inward toward the human interior and the motives behind wealth-love.
Hoarding gold and silver and withholding them establishes the attachment for which the next ayah heats that treasure and brands its owners.
Lightning gives just enough intermittent light to walk before darkness makes people stop, a natural parallel to the instant spark that cannot become the section's lasting morning.
The retreating night supplies the darkness-side of the transition completed by the oath to morning in 74:34.
وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا أَسْفَرَ depicts morning unveiling its light, a direct ص ب ح formulation of the image's durable replacement of darkness.
The withdrawing night is the immediate counterpart to morning's breathing in 81:18 and completes that light-over-darkness scene.
The lowest heaven is adorned بِمَصَابِيحَ, using the source dictionary's lamp word for fixed celestial lights rather than sparks that vanish in the air.
Celestial مَصَابِيح adorn the sky and also serve as missiles, combining lasting lamps with moving fiery projectiles in one image.
The preceding sparks are compared to yellow camels, extending the airborne-spark scene while unexpectedly returning it to an animal form.
A piercing شِهَاب pursues the one who snatches a hearing; the fiery object named as a useful carried ember in 27:7 becomes an airborne projectile.
One brought from death to life is given a light by which to walk among people, while another remains in darkness; resurrection, guidance, and useful illumination meet without a literal flame.
On Judgment Day believers' light runs before them and they ask God to complete it, an enduring eschatological light set against sparks that do not illuminate.
People in the Fire have exhaling and inhaling; this places breath inside the fire scene, echoing the section's linkage of dabh-breath with heat and ash.
The question about the greatest losers in deeds opens a Quranic counterpart to the section's choice between an undertaking that catches and a spark spent in vain.
Their effort goes astray in worldly life while they think they are doing well, precisely rendering a mind that strikes the “flint of misguidance.”
Consultation over the matter, followed by resolve and trust, gives a positive Quranic form of the source dictionary's figurative striking of an affair through examination and planning.
The queen refuses to decide her affair before counsel is present, another concrete instance of carefully “striking” a matter in the source dictionary's figurative sense.
The different ء ن س usage فَإِنْ آنَسْتُمْ مِنْهُمْ رُشْدًا means perceiving sound judgment in orphans; it links perception to the image's question of whether human thought finds guidance or error.
After Satan has led multitudes astray, the rebuke “did you not reason?” gives the section's “flint of misguidance” an explicit Quranic formulation.
Hell is then identified as the promised destination, connecting the failure of reason in 36:62 to fire.
The misled are commanded to burn there because of their rejection, completing the sequence from failed reasoning to destructive fire.
